name: Minobasco (Shokoba)
description: Minobasco (often associated with the name 'Shokoba') is a specialized, modern variant of the traditional Italian fishing game 'Escoba' (or Scopa). It is unique for its use of colorful plastic 'Gemstones' as scoring tokens and its simplified point-capture rules aimed at a faster, more competitive pace. Like Scopa, players use cards from their hand to capture sums of cards from the table, but with an emphasis on 'Shokoba'â€”clearing the entire table for a bonus point.

history.origins: A modern evolution of 'Escoba de 15' (Spanish/Italian fishing). The 'Minobasco' branding emerged in Central Europe (Liechtenstein/Switzerland) as a boutique card set in the late 20th century.
timeline: 1980s: Traditional Escoba is re-branded with 'Gemstone' scoring for younger players.
1990s: Small-scale production of 'Shokoba' sets occurs in regional clubs.
Present: Played as a quick family game in specific Mediterranean and Alpine communities.
21st Century: Noted for its similarity to the Japanese 'Hanafuda' and Korean 'Go-Stop' in its fishing mechanics.
history.cultural: Represents the 'Gamerization' of century-old folk games for the modern tabletop market.
history.evolution: The game moved from pen-and-paper scoring to a physical economy (Gemstones), making it more tactile and social.

setup.dealing: Each player receives 3 cards. 4 cards are placed face-up on the table. The deal is repeated until the deck is empty.

rules.objective: Score Gemstones by capturing table cards (by matching value or sum), by making a Shokoba (sweep) when you clear the table, and from end-of-round awards (most cards, most Coins/Diamonds, Settebello, Primiera). The first player or team to reach 11 Gemstones wins the game.
rules.gameplay:
1. **Capture**: Play a card from your hand. If its value matches a single card or the SUM of multiple cards on the table, you capture them.
2. **Example**: A player plays a 7; they can take a 7 from the table, or a 4 and a 3, or a 5 and a 2.
3. **Shokoba!**: If you capture ALL remaining cards on the table, you shout 'SHOKOBA!' and win 1 Gemstone immediately.
keyRules: Capture by playing a card that matches one table card or the sum of several table cards; if both match, take the single card.
When a capture is possible you must capture.
Shokoba: clearing the entire table in one play scores 1 Gemstone.

strategy.basic: Prioritize the 7 of Diamonds. It is the most valuable card in the deck and contributes to the 'Most Diamonds' and 'Preme' points. Never play it unless you are certain it will be captured.
strategy.intermediate: Preventing Shokoba: If there is only one card left on the table (e.g., a 4), and you can't capture it, DON'T play a card that sums to a high value. Play a card that leaves the table with values that are hard to sum for the next player (like two small cards instead of one high one).
strategy.advanced: The 'Diamond Sweep': If you are trailing in points, focus entirely on the 'Most Diamonds' category. Even if you lose individual tricks, capturing 6 or 7 Diamonds will guarantee you 2 points at the end of the round (Diamond count + 7 of Diamonds).
tips: Count the 7s. There are only four. If three have been played, the last 7 becomes a powerful 'Shokoba' tool.
If playing in teams, watch what your partner leaves on the table. Try to 'setup' a sum for them if you suspect they have a high-value card.

variations.name: Standard Minobasco
variations.description: Two to four players; capture by value or sum; Shokoba (sweep) awards 1 Gemstone; first to 11 Gemstones wins.

variations.name: Team play (4 players)
variations.description: Four players in two teams; partners sit opposite; same rules, team score first to 11 Gemstones.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Team mode shares base engine; partnerships handled at config level.

scoring.description: Be the first to collect 11 Gemstones (points). Points from Shokoba sweeps, most cards, most Diamonds/Coins, Settebello (7 of Coins), and Primiera.
scoring.winCondition: First player or team to reach 11 or more Gemstones wins.
